subject: biology
title: Biotechnology and food production
key_idea: (Separate science) Biotechnology helps feed a growing population. The fungus Fusarium is grown in a fermenter to make mycoprotein, a protein-rich food. Genetic modification gives crops useful features such as pest resistance, but it raises concerns.

blocks.text: **Mycoprotein** is a protein-rich food made from the fungus Fusarium. This section covers how it is grown in a fermenter and why the conditions matter.

items.meaning: A protein-rich food made from the fungus Fusarium.
A large vessel in which microorganisms are grown under controlled conditions.

diagram.alt: Five steps in making mycoprotein: sterilise the fermenter, add Fusarium and glucose, bubble in air, keep the temperature suitable, collect the mycoprotein.

items: The fermenter is **sterilised** to kill microorganisms. Otherwise they compete with the fungus for food and oxygen, make toxins, or cause disease.
Glucose and oxygen are used for aerobic respiration, which releases energy for growth.
Bubbles of air supply oxygen and move materials around the fermenter.
Moving materials around gives the fungus enough food, enough oxygen and a suitable temperature, and removes carbon dioxide.
A suitable temperature is kept so the fungus grows faster.

blocks.text: Mycoprotein is a source of protein, but its protein content per 100 g can be lower than that of meat. More of it must then be eaten to get the same mass of protein.

blocks.label: Mass of mycoprotein for the same protein
blocks.formula: mass of mycoprotein = (protein in 100 g of meat ÷ protein in 100 g of mycoprotein) × 100
where: protein in 100 g of meat, in g
protein in 100 g of mycoprotein, in g

diagram.alt: Calculate the mass of mycoprotein that gives the same mass of protein as 100 g of chicken.
diagram.question: 100 g of chicken contains {P} g of protein. 100 g of mycoprotein contains {Q} g of protein. What mass of mycoprotein contains the same mass of protein as 100 g of chicken?

items: Fusarium is grown in a sterile fermenter to make mycoprotein.
Glucose and oxygen are used in aerobic respiration to release energy for growth.
Mixing keeps food, oxygen and temperature suitable throughout.

blocks.text: **Genetic modification** changes a crop's genes to give it a useful feature. For example, a gene from a bacterium that makes a toxin killing insects can be inserted into a crop plant.

items: Resistance to disease, pests, frost or drought.
Taste, flavour and colour.
Yield, so more food can be produced.

blocks.text: Sort the points below into advantages and disadvantages of crops modified to resist insect pests.

diagram.alt: Sort statements about insect-resistant GM crops into advantages and disadvantages.
diagram.prompt: Advantage or disadvantage of insect-resistant GM crops?

items.text: Less crop damage, so a higher yield
Less insecticide needs to be used
Insects may develop resistance to the toxin
Genes could be transferred to other species, such as weeds
GM seeds can be more expensive to buy
Farmers rely on GM seed companies

items: Other concerns include long-term effects, allergic reactions and ethical objections to moving genes between species.
Some people worry about harm to useful insects, food chains and biodiversity.
GM crops can have a larger yield and resistance to pests, so more food is produced and fewer chemicals are needed.
Concerns include gene transfer to other plants, resistance developing and cost.
In a discussion question, give both advantages and disadvantages.

checks.q: Explain why the fermenter is sterilised before Fusarium is grown in it.
checks.a: To kill microorganisms, which would compete with the fungus for food or oxygen, make toxins or cause disease, so the mycoprotein is not contaminated.

checks.q: Explain why Fusarium needs glucose and oxygen.
checks.a: For aerobic respiration, which releases energy for growth.

checks.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of growing GM crops that are resistant to insects.
checks.a: Advantage: less crop damage, so a higher yield (or less insecticide is needed). Disadvantage: genes could spread to other plants, or insects could develop resistance (or the seeds cost more).

worked_example.question:
Mycoprotein is a protein-rich food. Mycoprotein is made from the fungus Fusarium. The fungus is grown in a fermenter.

Explain why the fermenter is sterilised before use.
answer_points: It kills microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, viruses or microbes).
These would compete for food or oxygen, make toxins, be pathogens or kill the Fusarium. Allow: so the mycoprotein is safe to eat.
worked_example.tip: One mark for what the sterilising does and one for why that matters. "Germs" is ignored.

worked_example.question:
Some crop plants have been genetically modified to be resistant to insect pests.

Explain the advantages and disadvantages of producing genetically modified crop plants.
answer_points: Advantage: less crop damage, so a higher yield and more food for people.
Advantage: crop plants are less likely to have diseases spread by insects, so less pesticide is used.
Advantage: more profit, so more income for developing countries.
Disadvantage: concerns about long-term effects, and ethical concerns about moving genes between species.
Disadvantage: genes could be transferred to weeds, which could then compete with crop plants.
Disadvantage: GM seeds could be more expensive, and insects may evolve so the crops are no longer resistant.
worked_example.tip: Full marks need more than one advantage and more than one disadvantage, with one of each clearly explained.

worked_example.question:
Over the whole world the demand for food to feed humans is increasing.
Genetic modification (GM) is one method that humans are using to try and produce more food.

Scientists can use GM to alter the features of crops.
One feature is crop yield.
Suggest two other features of crops they could change.
answer_points: Any two from: disease resistance, frost resistance, pest resistance, drought resistance.
Also credited: taste, flavour, colour, or making vaccines.
worked_example.tip: Yield and size of fruit are ignored, because the question has already used yield.

worked_example.question:
Penicillin can be produced in fermenters.

Explain why the temperature in the fermenter must be controlled.
answer_points: Respiration by the organisms produces heat.
The organisms contain enzymes.
Enzymes are denatured by too much heat.
The temperature is kept at the optimum, so the organisms are not killed.
This gives the maximum yield of product.
worked_example.tip: Any three points score the marks.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Fermenters are used on a large scale to make useful products from bacteria and fungi.

items: Bacteria make **insulin**.
The fungus Penicillium makes **penicillin**.
The fungus Fusarium makes **mycoprotein**.

rows: Respiration releases heat. Too much heat denatures enzymes, so the temperature is kept at the optimum for the greatest yield.
The enzymes work best at their optimum pH, so it is monitored and kept constant.
The organisms need oxygen for aerobic respiration, which releases energy for growth.
Glucose and other nutrients are needed for the organisms to grow and make the product.
Waste, such as carbon dioxide and heat, is removed so that it does not harm the organisms.

worked_example.question:
Industrial fermenters are used to grow microorganisms. These microorganisms produce penicillin, an antibiotic that is used to treat bacterial infections.

Explain how named conditions in an industrial fermenter are controlled.
answer_points: Oxygen is provided for respiration, using an aerator or air inlet.
The temperature is kept at the optimum and overheating is prevented, using a temperature monitor and a water jacket.
The pH is kept at the optimum, using a pH monitor and an inlet for acid or alkali.
Contamination is prevented to keep the fermenter aseptic, using an air filter and by sterilising or steam cleaning before use.
The contents are mixed so that nutrients, oxygen and heat are spread evenly, using a stirrer or paddles.
worked_example.tip: Each mark is for a named condition, then for the method used to control it.

blocks.text: Any microorganism can be grown in an industrial fermenter, not only Fusarium. These conditions are controlled.

items: **Aseptic precautions**: the fermenter is sterilised, for example with steam, and air is filtered, so other microorganisms cannot contaminate it.
**Nutrients**: a nutrient broth supplies food for growth.
**Optimum temperature and pH**, kept steady by monitors, a cooling jacket and the addition of acid or alkali.
**Oxygenation**: air is bubbled in so the organisms can respire aerobically.
**Agitation**: stirring spreads nutrients, oxygen and heat evenly.
